memoryText: For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Luke 2:11 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
An angel says these words to shepherds in the dark, on a hillside outside Bethlehem. It is the message at the center of the Christmas story and of the Gospel.

“For unto you.” The news is personal. The angel does not say, “For the world in general.” He says, “For you.” The first people to hear it were common workers in the fields. The gospel comes to people where they are, and it is addressed to each of us.

“Is born this day.” The word “today” is one of Luke’s favorites. Salvation is not only a future hope. It has arrived in time and space, on a particular day, in a real town. God has acted in history.

“In the city of David.” The Savior comes in the line of the great king. Every promise about David’s throne is being fulfilled in this child.

“A Savior.” The word means rescuer. He is born not just to teach or to inspire but to save. Matthew told us he would save his people from their sins. Luke says that he is a Savior for “all the people.”

“Who is Christ the Lord.” Christ means the anointed king. Lord means the one who rules, and it is the word the Greek Old Testament used for God himself. The baby in the manger is God’s anointed king and God himself.

When you feel that the gospel is too big or too distant, say this verse. It was spoken first to shepherds, and it is for you.
weekInReview: This week you began the Gospel of Luke. You read Luke’s careful preface, the promise of two births, and the songs of Mary and Zechariah, which celebrate God’s keeping of every promise. You saw the Savior born in a manger and heard the angels announce good news to shepherds. You watched Simeon and Anna recognize him in the temple. You followed John’s call to repentance, Jesus’ baptism and temptation, and his first sermon in Nazareth, where he read Isaiah and said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled.” You saw him call sinners, eat with outcasts, and spend a whole night in prayer before choosing the Twelve. The Sermon on the Plain called you to love your enemies and build on the rock. Psalm 113 gave you the words behind the Magnificat: the God who is high above all stoops to raise the poor from the dust.
reflectionQuestions: Luke records that the angels’ first announcement was to shepherds. What does that tell you about the kind of people the gospel is for, and how might it change who you notice this week?
Jesus read Isaiah 61 in Nazareth and said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.” How does Jesus fulfill the good news for the poor, the captives, and the blind?
Mary said, “Let it be to me according to your word.” Where do you most need to say that to God right now?
prayerPrompts: Thank God that to us a Savior is born.
Thank him that the good news is for all people.
